data.title: Laverock unveils new in vivo programmes in oncology
data.description:
Laverock Therapeutics has announced new in vivo programmes spanning CAR‑T and genetic medicine, expanding its therapeutic pipeline beyond ex vivo cell therapies. The company said the move strengthens its ability to tackle major challenges in oncology and genetic disease. Its programmable gene control platform enables tunable and multiplex control of endogenous targets and transgenic payloads.

The technology has already been validated in several cell therapy applications, including armoured autologous T cells and iPSC‑derived macrophages targeting solid tumours. Laverock said its in vivo programmes will improve efficacy, safety, accessibility and scalability for CAR‑T, while supporting development across high unmet‑need indications in genetic medicine.

Solid tumours represent 90% of cancer cases, and the company believes its platform is well suited to overcoming the inhibitory factors of the tumour micro‑environment.

In genetic medicine, Laverock will use in vivo gene silencing through direct delivery of gene editing tools. This approach aims to support therapy development for nervous system disorders and metabolic disease. The company said its technology is differentiated by its ability to control multiple targets or pathways simultaneously with precision and context‑specific gene expression.

David Venables, CEO of Laverock Therapeutics, said: “Building on our success in developing ex vivo therapeutics, we are extremely excited to announce the launch of our in vivo programmes, and realise the benefits these cutting edge technologies can bring to patients.”

He added: “This area is highly innovative, and our platform can provide a key element to realising its potential.”

Laverock said industry interest is growing in therapies that can be delivered directly to patients while maintaining precision and safety. The company has several technology partnerships and is open to new collaborations.

data.title: SMC accepts AQUIPTA for eligible migraine patients in Scotland
data.description:
AbbVie has announced that the SMC has accepted AQUIPTA (atogepant) for acute migraine treatment in adults, only if at least two triptans were previously tried without sufficient effect, or triptans were contraindicated or not tolerated, and NSAIDs and paracetamol were also tried but did not work well enough. Suitable patients can now be prescribed atogepant for acute use within NHS Scotland.

The acceptance follows NICE’s recommendation published on June 30, 2026 and the MHRA’s marketing authorisation granted on April 22, 2026. Migraine affects around 600,000 adults in Scotland and is the second leading global cause of years lived with disability among people aged 15 to 49 years.

Migraine is widely misunderstood as merely a headache. Symptoms include recurrent moderate to severe throbbing head pain, nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound. The condition can disrupt daily life and prevent people from carrying out everyday activities. It also carries a considerable emotional burden, with many people reporting stigma and dismissal of their symptoms.

Rob Music, CEO at the Migraine Trust, said: “Access to appropriate migraine care can be seriously inconsistent, creating a postcode lottery. We know that many people with migraine struggle to access the treatments they need or had to face long waits to see a specialist before finding the option that works best for them. A greater variety of treatments available is essential for migraine care and we therefore welcome today’s update from the SMC, which adds an additional treatment option for eligible migraine patients.”

Dr David Watson, GPwER Headache, Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, explained: “Migraine is a common and often disabling neurological condition. While existing treatments help many people, not everyone responds well or is able to tolerate current options. Having an additional treatment available is welcome news for people living with migraine in Scotland, offering greater choice and helping clinicians tailor treatment to individual patient needs.”

The recommendation is supported by results from ECLIPSE, a pivotal phase 3 study in which 24.3% of patients treated with atogepant achieved pain freedom at 2 hours post dose following the first migraine attack, compared with 13.1% for placebo. There were no individual TEAEs with an incidence ≥ 2% for the first attack in the double‑blind period.

Rachael Millward, Medical Director, AbbVie UK, added: “We are pleased that SMC has accepted atogepant as an acute treatment option for eligible migraine patients in Scotland. Migraine is a highly complex neurological condition that can significantly affect daily life, and we remain committed to supporting better outcomes for people living with the condition”

data.title: RougeTx launches with $58 million series A financing for HHT therapy
data.description:
RougeTx has launched with a $58 million series A financing to advance RTX‑001, a potential once‑daily oral treatment designed to restore blood vessel stability in HHT. The round was co‑led by BGV, Angelini Ventures and Kurma Partners, with participation from Epidarex Capital, Vesalius Biocapital Partners, ROM Utrecht Region, p53 Invest and Kerna Ventures.

The funding will support RTX‑001 as it progresses toward first‑in‑human development. HHT is the second most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by abnormal blood vessel formation known as AVMs. These can lead to recurrent nose and gastrointestinal bleeding, iron deficiency, chronic anemia and serious complications affecting major organs. There are currently no approved therapies for HHT.

Andrew Lightfoot, Chief Executive Officer at RougeTx, said: “RTX-001 is designed to stabilize fragile blood vessels by restoring pericyte attachment. The data we have generated for RTX-001 gives us a strong foundation as we move toward the clinic. This financing also allows us to explore where the same biology may impact other vascular diseases.”

Franck Lebrin, Co‑Founder and Scientific Advisor at RougeTx, remarked: “RougeTx represents the culmination of more than 20 years of research, initially at Inserm and over the past decade in my laboratory at Leiden University Medical Center. I am excited by the opportunity to bring a novel treatment to the HHT community.”

Sandra Glucksmann, Executive Chair at RougeTx, noted: “For too long, people living with HHT have faced a serious, lifelong disease with no approved treatment options. RougeTx was founded with a commitment to this community and a belief that advances in vascular biology can finally make a meaningful difference for patients and families. We are grateful to our investors for their support and shared commitment to our mission.”

RougeTx’s periSCOPE platform is designed to expand the pipeline beyond HHT, identifying new treatment opportunities in diseases driven by vascular instability and supporting development of small‑molecule therapies based on shared underlying biology.

data.title: Lundbeck presents phase 1b data for Lu AF28996 in advanced Parkinson’s disease
data.description:
Lundbeck has reported results from an open‑label phase 1b trial evaluating Lu AF28996, an investigational oral prodrug of a D1‑like/D2‑like dopamine receptor agonist, in people with advanced Parkinson’s disease whose motor symptoms remained sub‑optimally controlled despite optimized non‑invasive treatment. The findings are being presented at MDS 2026 in Seoul.

Parkinson’s disease involves progressive degeneration of dopamine‑producing neurons. Many people develop motor complications over time, including fluctuations between Good ON‑time and OFF‑time, and treatment‑related dyskinesia. Existing options for advanced disease often require invasive procedures or continuous drug delivery, highlighting the need for effective non‑invasive approaches.

Tarek Samad, Executive Vice President and Head of Research & Development at Lundbeck, said: “Many people with advanced Parkinson’s disease continue to experience motor fluctuations and dyskinesia that can significantly affect daily life. We are encouraged by the phase Ib results with Lu AF28996, including the improvements observed alongside substantial reductions in levodopa dose. With the DARE2 phase II trial now underway, we are taking the next step in evaluating its potential in a larger, randomized and controlled study.”

In part B of the trial, 34 participants received Lu AF28996 twice daily for six weeks, with 25 continuing for an optional 12‑week extension. Most treatment‑emergent adverse events were mild, with no unexpected safety signals. The most common events were nausea, dizziness and fall.

At baseline, participants experienced a mean of 9.5 hours of Good ON‑time, 4.7 hours of OFF‑time and 1.8 hours of ON‑time with troublesome dyskinesia. At Weeks 6 and 18, Good ON‑time increased by 3.6 and 3.4 hours, OFF‑time decreased by 2.3 and 2.0 hours, and ON‑time with troublesome dyskinesia decreased by 1.2 and 1.4 hours. Dyskinesia severity, measured by UDysRS, improved by 8.5 points at Week 6 and 14.5 points at Week 18. Mean daily levodopa dose fell by 53.4% at Week 6 and 29.2% at Week 18.

Among participants with at least one hour per day of troublesome dyskinesia at baseline, ON‑time with troublesome dyskinesia decreased by 2.3 hours at Week 6 and 2.8 hours at Week 18. The exploratory trial involved a limited number of participants and no placebo or active comparator.

DARE2, a phase 2 randomised, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial, is now underway and will evaluate Lu AF28996 in approximately 150 adults. The primary endpoint is change from baseline to Week 19 in daily Good ON‑time. Recruitment has begun in the US, with additional sites planned across Europe and Japan.

Lu AF28996 is not approved by the FDA or any other regulatory agency, and its efficacy and safety have not been established.

data.title: MINT study results strengthen real‑world evidence for mogamulizumab
data.description:
Kyowa Kirin International has announced final results from the German MINT study evaluating mogamulizumab in patients with MF and SS. Presented at the EORTC‑CLTG Annual Meeting 2026, the findings represent one of the largest real‑world evaluations of the therapy in Germany and add to evidence supporting its use in routine practice.

MINT was a company‑sponsored, multicentric, non‑interventional real‑world study across 18 centres. It assessed outcomes in a broad patient population, including clinically relevant subgroups such as LCT and fMF, and stratified by disease stage and MAR status.

MF and SS are forms of CTCL, a type of non‑Hodgkin’s lymphoma that manifests on the skin. Symptoms can include persistent rashes, changes in skin colour and plaques or tumours. These visible symptoms can significantly affect patients’ quality of life.

Professor Chalid Assaf, Director of the Department of Dermatology and Venereology, Helios Klinikum Krefeld, said: “For patients living with mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome, understanding how treatments perform outside the controlled setting of clinical trials is critically important.

“The final MINT results demonstrate meaningful clinical outcomes across a broad patient population treated in routine practice and highlight the value of collaborative real-world research in helping clinicians make informed treatment decisions.”

The final analysis included 109 patients, with a median follow‑up of 25.2 months. Most had advanced disease at treatment initiation. The study reported a median TTNT of 14.9 months, a best overall response rate of 62.4% and a median progression‑free survival of 20.2 months. Median overall survival was not estimable due to the limited number of deaths observed.

Exploratory analyses showed best overall response rates of 54.5% in patients with LCT and 50.0% in patients with fMF. Additional analyses by disease stage reported best overall response rates of 50% in early‑stage disease and 64.8% in advanced disease. Disease control rate in patients with MAR was 95.7%.

Patients also experienced improvements in quality of life, with median Skindex‑29 scores improving by 38.5% from baseline to Month 12.

Dr Azeem Danish, Medical Affairs Director, DACH, Kyowa Kirin, explained: “MINT provides valuable real-world evidence from Germany on the use of mogamulizumab across the heterogeneous population of patients with mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome, including clinically relevant subgroups that are often underrepresented in clinical trials. By evaluating time-to-next-treatment as a clinically meaningful outcome, the study offers practical insights that can support CTCL specialists in making informed, individualised treatment decisions.”

Investigators concluded that mogamulizumab demonstrated a safety profile comparable to the pivotal phase 3 MAVORIC study, with grade 3 or higher treatment‑related adverse events reported in 38.5% of patients. Serious treatment‑related adverse events leading to discontinuation occurred in 22.0% of patients.

data.title: SMC accepts vutrisiran for eligible patients in Scotland
data.description:
Alnylam UK Limited has welcomed a Scottish Medicines Consortium decision to accept vutrisiran for adults with ATTR‑CM, enabling eligible patients to access AMVUTTRA through NHS Scotland. The therapy is the first long‑acting disease‑modifying option to target the underlying biology of the condition.

Vutrisiran is administered as a subcutaneous injection every three months and delivers rapid, sustained knockdown of transthyretin proteins, observed from six weeks and persisting up to 30 months.

An estimated 1,800 people in Scotland could be living with ATTR‑CM, including diagnosed and undiagnosed patients. Vutrisiran is also indicated for hereditary ATTR amyloidosis in adults with stage 1 or 2 polyneuropathy.

Dr Joanne Simpson, Cardiologist, Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, Glasgow, said: “The SMC’s acceptance represents a significant step forward for patients and clinicians in Scotland. ATTR-CM is a progressive condition causing heart failure and reduced quality of life. Vutrisiran targets the underlying biology of the disease and represents an important additional disease modifying treatment option for eligible patients. This decision is meaningful progress in management of ATTR-CM, whilst continued efforts to improve early recognition, diagnosis and timely referral are essential.”

ATTR‑CM affects around 1,500 people across the UK, though under‑diagnosis means the true number is likely higher. It occurs when misfolded transthyretin proteins accumulate in the heart, forming amyloid deposits that stiffen the muscle and impair its ability to pump blood. If untreated, the disease is associated with high mortality.

Katharine McIntosh, Chief Executive Office at Cardiomyopathy UK, explained: “The SMC’s decision on vutrisiran is very welcome news for people living with ATTR-CM in Scotland. ATTR-CM is a rare, progressive and life-limiting condition that can affect physical health and mental wellbeing, and we were pleased to be able to share our patient community’s experiences as part of the assessment. Having another treatment option – one that targets the underlying cause, and that can often be self-administered at home – gives eligible patients greater choice.”

Kate Taylor, Chief Executive Office at Amyloidosis UK, said: “ATTR with cardiomyopathy can have a significant impact on people’s lives and on those closest to them. People can face a long journey to diagnosis, highlighting the importance of greater awareness and earlier recognition of the condition so that people can receive appropriate care as soon as possible.”

With this recommendation, vutrisiran becomes the first treatment accepted by the SMC for both ATTR‑CM and hereditary ATTR with stage 1 or 2 polyneuropathy. The decision follows NICE’s recommendation in England and Wales in December 2025.

Phil Davey, General Manager, Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, UK, Ireland and Canada, added: “We welcome the SMC’s decision, which represents an important milestone for people living with ATTR-CM in Scotland. At Alnylam, we are committed to translating the potential of RNAi into meaningful treatment options for patients, and this recommendation is an important step on that journey. We would like to thank the SMC, the patient community, clinicians and NHS Scotland for their continued collaboration in helping make this treatment available.”

data.title: NHS Blood and Transplant partners with Northwest Biotherapeutics
data.description:
Northwest Biotherapeutics and NHS Blood and Transplant have agreed a collaboration to support production of DCVax-L, a personalised immunotherapy for solid tumour cancers. The partnership will begin in Leeds and Oxford, with plans to extend services across England.

DCVax-L uses a patient’s own immune system to recognise and attack cancer. Each treatment is manufactured individually using immune cells collected from the patient and material from their tumour.

Under the agreement, NHS Blood and Transplant will provide specialist services to collect and process patients’ immune cells for DCVax-L manufacturing. This includes leukapheresis, which collects the white blood cells needed for the personalised treatment, alongside specialist cell processing and handling delivered by Cellular and Molecular Therapies teams.

The process uses leukapheresis, an established procedure that collects specific white blood cells while returning remaining blood components to the body.

Working with Northwest Biotherapeutics and Advent Bioservices, NHS Blood and Transplant will help strengthen UK infrastructure supporting DCVax-L production.

The organisations are also exploring opportunities to expand the collaboration across NHS Blood and Transplant’s network of specialist facilities. This could reduce the distances patients and families need to travel.

Ms Linda Powers, CEO of Northwest Biotherapeutics, said: “NHSBT’s impressive expertise and facilities for advanced therapies are at the forefront of the field. We are very excited about collaborating with them on our DCVax-L personalised immune therapies for cancer. We believe NHSBT’s capabilities can significantly enhance the scale-up and accessibility of DCVax-L.”

Dr James Griffin, Medical Director NHS Blood and Transplant, explained: “The collaboration forms part of ongoing work between NHSBT, NWBio and Advent Bioservices to strengthen the infrastructure supporting the production of DCVax-L in the UK. We aim to help make cutting edge advanced therapies more accessible.

“Alongside the planned expansion of the existing therapeutic apheresis and cell processing model, the organisations are also exploring opportunities for broader collaboration involving NHSBT’s specialist laboratory and advanced therapies capabilities.”

data.title: Atrogi reports human data showing muscle gains with ATR‑258
data.description:
Atrogi has announced positive human data for ATR‑258, its first‑in‑class oral GRK2‑biased β2‑adrenergic modulator designed to improve muscle function and body composition.

In an 8‑week investigator‑initiated study in 13 overweight or obese adults, the therapy was well tolerated and associated with an approximately 13% mean improvement in lower‑extremity muscle power. Participants also saw statistically significant reductions in fat mass and increases in lean mass.

The open‑label, single‑arm trial, led by Professor Morten Hostrup, evaluated three ascending dose levels of ATR‑258. Treatment resulted in a mean 1.1 kg reduction in fat mass and a 0.8 kg increase in lean mass. Atrogi said the profile highlights the therapy’s potential in metabolic and muscle‑related diseases with high unmet need.

Professor Tore Bengtsson, Chief Scientific Officer and Founder of Atrogi, said: “These first clinical data give us important confidence that our approach is translating. To see fat loss alongside an increase in lean muscle mass and improvement in muscle function represents a truly differentiated profile, and is highly encouraging.”

He added: “Beyond muscle-sparing weight loss, we believe this mechanism also warrants investigation in sarcopenia and rare diseases marked by substantial muscle loss and weakness.”

The findings build on a landmark Cell publication from 2025, which established Atrogi’s GRK2‑biased signalling approach and detailed first‑in‑human safety data from a 69‑subject phase 1 trial. The new results provide first human proof‑of‑mechanism and support plans to begin a phase 2 trial in 2027.

Professor Morten Hostrup, Principal Investigator, commented: “As a researcher who has long studied β2-adrenergic receptor signalling in skeletal muscle, I was curious whether a biased, highly selective GRK2 modulator could harness this pathway differently – driving beneficial changes in muscle mass and function without the trade-offs seen with classical β2-agonists.”

He continued: “What struck me most was the magnitude of the signal in lower-extremity power.”

Paul Little, Chief Executive Officer at Atrogi, said: “These results are a major step forward for Atrogi and we thank everyone involved. We are a phase 2‑ready biotech with a first‑in‑class, next‑generation oral GRK2‑biased β2‑adrenergic modulator.”

He added: “We now have human data pointing to a unique profile in metabolic health in a broad context where muscle becomes medicine.”

data.title: Bespak and SNBL agree global access deal for FDA‑approved nasal device
data.description:
Bespak has signed an MOU with SNBL to provide immediate and exclusive global access to SNBL’s proprietary nasal dry powder delivery device for developers of novel intranasal therapies.

The agreement strengthens Bespak’s nasal drug delivery offering, which now spans liquid, soft mist and dry powder products from early development through to commercial supply.

The device will be marketed as the Air Pump Unit Dose Intranasal Powder device. It is single‑use, compact and easy to carry, delivering powder intranasally from a drug‑containing nozzle attached to a simple user‑activated air pump. It does not require patients to coordinate breathing during administration. The design supports high dose loading, enhanced stability, improved bioavailability and deposition targeting.

Nasal drug delivery is attracting growing interest for CNS and systemic routes, with potential applications in pain, neurological conditions, degenerative diseases and vaccines.

SNBL’s device, approved as part of Satsuma Pharmaceuticals’ Atzumi migraine treatment in April 2025, is one of only three FDA‑approved dry powder nasal devices available. Bespak is the chosen contract manufacturer for filling and assembly of Atzumi, offering customers a faster and lower‑risk route to approval in the US and other regulated markets.

Chris Hirst, CEO of Bespak, said: “Nasal drug delivery is entering an exciting new era, with developers looking for solutions that can deliver next-generation therapies effectively while also meeting patients’ needs for greater convenience and ease of use.

“Our agreement with SNBL strengthens Bespak’s ability to respond to that need, bringing together an FDA-approved dry powder nasal device with our capabilities in formulation, development and commercial manufacturing. Our ambition is to help our customers unlock the potential of nasal delivery and bring more nasal drug breakthroughs to patients.”

data.title: NEMLUVIO data show sustained three‑year responses in atopic dermatitis
data.description:
Galderma has announced new NEMLUVIO data to be presented at Fall Clinical 2026, including a post‑hoc analysis from the ARCADIA LTE study showing that most adults and adolescents aged 12 and older who responded at Week 16 maintained deep and lasting improvements in skin lesions and itch for up to three years. The findings add to growing evidence supporting long‑term efficacy in moderate to severe atopic dermatitis.

The ARCADIA LTE analysis evaluated 295 early responders who continued treatment through maintenance and extension phases. At Week 56, 77% achieved clear or almost clear skin or at least a 90% improvement in disease severity. This was sustained to Week 152, where 76% achieved IGA 0/1, 80% achieved EASI‑90 and 50% achieved EASI‑100. At Week 152, 80% also reached an itch‑free or nearly itch‑free state.

Nemluvio was well tolerated, with no new safety signals. The results align with previously collected long‑term safety and efficacy data in adults and adolescents with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis.

Bill Andriopoulos, Ph.D., Head of Global Medical Affairs, Galderma, said: “Patients and physicians increasingly expect more from treatment than temporary symptom relief. The data presented at Fall Clinical reinforce our confidence in Nemluvio’s potential to deliver durable disease control, with evidence spanning deep and sustained responses on skin and itch through three years in adults and adolescents, and a consistent long-term safety and efficacy profile.”

A separate interim analysis of 1,903 patients in the overall ARCADIA LTE population showed sustained improvements through Week 152, including up to 91% achieving EASI‑75, up to 75% achieving EASI‑90 and up to 67% achieving IGA 0/1. Up to 88% achieved clinically meaningful itch relief and up to 92% reported improvements in dermatology‑related quality of life.

Sarina Elmariah, M.D., Dermatologist and Itch Specialist, explained: “As progress in this high-burden disease area accelerates, we are challenged to aim higher in atopic dermatitis care. These new three-year results are encouraging for Nemluvio, adding to its growing body of evidence and highlighting its potential to help patients achieve meaningful long-term outcomes in atopic dermatitis.”

Phase 2 pediatric data will also be presented, showing meaningful and sustained improvements in children aged 2 to 11 years through Week 52. Additional OLYMPIA LTE findings demonstrated sustained improvements across multiple dimensions of prurigo nodularis burden through Week 148, with more than 85% achieving clinically meaningful itch improvement and 91% reporting improved quality of life.
